steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on Graph-of-Thought (GoT) reasoning in language models. Motivate it from the non-linear way humans think, place it against chain-of-thought and tree-of-thoughts prompting, explain the GoT framework and its multimodal version, and summarize the headline results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Human thinking is non-linear, not a simple chain
- LLMs and Chain-of-Thought prompting
- Limitation of sequential CoT; Tree-of-thoughts
- Our proposal: Graph-of-Thought
- GoT framework details and multimodal GoT
- Results summary

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Human thinking is non-linear
  - long recognized in cognition: more complex/non-linear than a sequential chain of thoughts (cite)
  - sudden leaps, connections between seemingly unrelated ideas -> novel insights, solutions
  - hallmark of creativity, reasoning, problem-solving; but a challenge for cognitive modeling
- LLMs and CoT
  - LLMs advancing at unprecedented pace: GPT-3, PaLM, GPT-4 (cite each) -> new era for NLP
  - recent studies (cite): CoT prompting unlocks reasoning ability
  - CoT = series of intermediate natural language rationales leading to final answer
  - Multimodal-CoT (cite): language + visual modalities, beyond limits of textual info
  - more related work in Appendix A
- Limitation of sequential CoT
  - prior CoT limited to text/visual info, reasoning as sequential thought chains
  - misses humans' jumping thought process, no complex structural info of reasoning thoughts
  - concurrent: Tree-of-thoughts (ToT) (cite), thought units, tree-like search
- Graph-of-Thought
  - human cognition beyond trees: intricate graph-like formations
  - intellect crafts elaborate thought graphs founded on linear thoughts
  - aim: concurrent assimilation of linear + nonlinear processes, not just segmented thought units
  - GoT: thought as chain and as graph; assumption: mind connects/recombines ideas non-sequentially
  - thought units = nodes, connections = edges -> realistic, logical modeling
- Framework
  - example in Figure 1
  - two-stage framework inspired by Multimodal-CoT (cite): rationales first, then answer
  - graph features of GoT added to text features in both stages
  - GoT built by Extract-Cluster-Coreference (ECC), simulating deduction
  - backbone T5 (cite); graph attention network encoder; gated fusion with original representation
  - multimodal GoT: text + GoT + visual features; FLAN-Alpaca (T5)-base and -large backbones
- Results
  - two-stage framework, fine-tuning LMs, text + thought graph + vision features
  - text-only AQUA-RAT (cite) and multimodal ScienceQA (cite)
  - beats ChatGPT (cite) by 9.28%, Multimodal-CoT (cite) by 2.40%, exceeds human performance
  - new state-of-the-art on ScienceQA test set, far fewer parameters

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
People who study human cognition have known for a long time that the way humans think is much more complex and non-linear than a simple chain of thoughts in sequence. Human thinking can make sudden leaps and connect ideas that look unrelated, and this can lead to new insights and solutions. This non-linear, jumping kind of thinking is a hallmark of human creativity, reasoning and problem solving. But it is also a big challenge when it comes to cognitive modeling and understanding.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently been advancing at a pace never seen before. With breakthroughs like GPT-3, PaLM and GPT-4, natural language processing has entered a new era of possibilities. Recent studies show that Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting can unlock the reasoning ability of LLMs. In CoT prompting there is a series of intermediate natural language rationales that lead to the final answer. Also, other work introduced Multimodal-CoT, which combines the language and visual modalities to help get past the limits of textual information. More related works are discussed in Appendix A.

Previous works on CoT prompting were limited to textual and visual information, and they often represented the human reasoning process as sequential thought chains. This does not model the jumping thought process of humans, and it does not put the complex structural information of reasoning thoughts into the model. The concurrent work Tree-of-thoughts (ToT) splits thoughts into thought units and models them as a tree-like search process.

- Graph-of-Thought
  - human cognition beyond tree structure: graph-like formations; intellect builds thought graphs on linear thoughts
  - aim: assimilate linear and nonlinear processes at once, not only segmented thought units
  - GoT models thought as chain and graph; mind connects and recombines ideas non-sequentially
  - thought units = nodes, connections = edges -> more realistic and logical modeling
- Framework
  - Figure 1 example; two-stage (rationale then answer), inspired by Multimodal-CoT (cite)
  - GoT graph features added to text features; ECC process; T5 backbone (cite); graph attention network + gated fusion
  - multimodal GoT with visual features; FLAN-Alpaca (T5)-base/-large
- Results
  - AQUA-RAT (cite), ScienceQA (cite); +9.28% over ChatGPT (cite), +2.40% over Multimodal-CoT (cite), above human
  - new SOTA on ScienceQA test set with far fewer parameters

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
People who study human cognition have known for a long time that the way humans think is much more complex and non-linear than a simple chain of thoughts in sequence. Human thinking can make sudden leaps and connect ideas that look unrelated, and this can lead to new insights and solutions. This non-linear, jumping kind of thinking is a hallmark of human creativity, reasoning and problem solving. But it is also a big challenge when it comes to cognitive modeling and understanding.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently been advancing at a pace never seen before. With breakthroughs like GPT-3, PaLM and GPT-4, natural language processing has entered a new era of possibilities. Recent studies show that Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting can unlock the reasoning ability of LLMs. In CoT prompting there is a series of intermediate natural language rationales that lead to the final answer. Also, other work introduced Multimodal-CoT, which combines the language and visual modalities to help get past the limits of textual information. More related works are discussed in Appendix A.

Previous works on CoT prompting were limited to textual and visual information, and they often represented the human reasoning process as sequential thought chains. This does not model the jumping thought process of humans, and it does not put the complex structural information of reasoning thoughts into the model. The concurrent work Tree-of-thoughts (ToT) splits thoughts into thought units and models them as a tree-like search process.

However, human cognition goes beyond a tree structure and shows intricate graph-like formations. Our view goes further than this, because we believe the human intellect can build elaborate thought graphs on top of linear thoughts. So we want to make it possible to assimilate linear and nonlinear cognitive processes at the same time, instead of just generating segmented thought units. To deal with this limitation, and different from ToT, we propose Graph-of-Thought (GoT), a new approach that models human thought processes not only as a chain but also as a graph. Our method assumes that the human mind works by connecting and recombining ideas in a non-sequential, graph way rather than by following a strict sequential chain. GoT represents thought units as nodes and the connections between thoughts as edges, so it captures the rich, non-sequential nature of human thinking and it makes the modeling of reasoning processes more realistic and logical.

Figure 1 shows an example of GoT reasoning. We adopted a two-stage reasoning framework, inspired by Multimodal-CoT. First it generates rationales, and then it generates the final answer based on the predicted rationales. Besides text features, we also integrate graph features of GoT in the rationale generation and in the answer inference. In more detail, GoT is first built with an Extract-Cluster-Coreference (ECC) process, which simulates the deductive process in human reasoning. Our backbone model is the T5 pre-trained language model. GoT is encoded with a graph attention network and then it is fused with the original representation with a gated fusion network.

We also present a multimodal GoT, which integrates visual features as well as the text features and GoT features. In our experiments we used FLAN-Alpaca (T5)-base and FLAN-Alpaca (T5)-large as the backbone models.

We implement GoT as a two-stage framework, fine-tuning language models and integrating text, thought graph and vision features to make the reasoning process more realistic and accurate. GoT does very well on both the text-only AQUA-RAT benchmark and the multimodal ScienceQA benchmark. It beats the accuracy of the online system ChatGPT by 9.28% and the strong baseline Multimodal-CoT by 2.40%, and it even goes beyond human performance, which sets a new state-of-the-art on the ScienceQA test set with far fewer parameters.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In the field of human cognition, it has long been recognized that the human thought process is far more complex and non-linear than a simple, sequential chain of thoughts could capture [1]. Human thinking is often characterized by sudden leaps and connections between seemingly unrelated ideas, which can lead to novel insights and solutions. This non-linear, jumping thought process is a hallmark of human creativity, reasoning, and problem-solving abilities. However, it also poses a significant challenge for cognitive modeling and understanding.

Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been advancing at an unprecedented pace. With breakthroughs such as GPT-3 [2], PaLM [3], and GPT-4 [4], natural language processing has entered a new era of possibilities. Recent studies [5,6,7] have shown that the reasoning ability of LLMs can be unlocked by Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, which involves a series of intermediate natural language rationales leading to the final answer. In addition, [8] have introduced Multimodal-CoT, which combines language and visual modalities to help surpass the limitations of textual information. More detailed related works can be found in Appendix A.

Previous works on Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, limited to textual and visual information, often represented the human reasoning process as sequential thought chains. This overlooks the modeling of humans' jumping thought process and neglects to incorporate the complex structural information of reasoning thoughts into the model. Concurrent work Tree-of-thoughts (ToT) [9] divides thoughts into thought units and models them as a tree-like search process.

Nevertheless, human cognition transcends this tree structure and exhibits intricate graph-like formations. Our perspective diverges further, as we believe the human intellect is capable of crafting elaborate thought graphs founded upon linear thoughts. We therefore aim to enable the concurrent assimilation of linear and nonlinear cognitive processes, going beyond the mere generation of segmented thought units. To address this limitation, and different from ToT, we propose Graph-of-Thought (GoT), a novel approach to modeling human thought processes not only as a chain but also as a graph. Our method assumes that the human mind works by connecting and recombining ideas in a non-sequential, graph fashion rather than following a strict sequential chain. By representing thought units as nodes and connections between thoughts as edges, GoT captures the rich, non-sequential nature of human thinking and allows a more realistic and logical modeling of reasoning processes.

An example of GoT reasoning is shown in Figure 1. Inspired by Multimodal-CoT [8], we adopt a two-stage reasoning framework, which first generates rationales and then generates the final answer based on the predicted rationales. In addition to text features, graph features of GoT are integrated during rationale generation and answer inference. Specifically, GoT is first constructed with an Extract-Cluster-Coreference (ECC) process, which simulates the deductive process in human reasoning. We use the T5 [10] pre-trained language model as our backbone model. GoT is encoded with a graph attention network and then fused with the original representation via a gated fusion network.

Furthermore, we also present a multimodal GoT, which integrates visual features in addition to text features and GoT features. For our experiments, we used both FLAN-Alpaca (T5)-base and FLAN-Alpaca (T5)-large as backbone models.

We implement GoT as a two-stage framework, fine-tuning language models and integrating text, thought graph, and vision features for a more realistic and accurate reasoning process. GoT shows exceptional performance on both the text-only AQUA-RAT [11] and the multimodal ScienceQA [12] benchmarks, surpassing the accuracy of the online system ChatGPT [4] by 9.28% and the strong baseline Multimodal-CoT [8] by 2.40%, and even exceeding human performance, establishing a new state-of-the-art on the ScienceQA test set with far fewer parameters.
